initial_observation.encounter_context: presented to the ophthalmology department of Jinnah Hospital Lahore
initial_observation.chief_complaint: 3 hour history of sudden, painless loss of vision in the left eye
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: The onset was abrupt, with no prior episodes of similar symptoms. The patient did not report any associated symptoms such as ocular redness, discharge, dizziness, headache, or blackouts. Additionally, she denied any history of photopsia (flashes of light) or vitreous floaters.
presenting_symptoms: sudden painless loss of vision in the left eye
known_prior_history: mother of three children who underwent cesarean section for each delivery; most recent was 3.5 months ago
started taking progestin-only pills after last delivery, took for 25 days before discontinuing
no history of smoking, previous contraceptive use, diabetes, or hypertension
personal and family history negative for congenital abnormalities or bleeding disorders

evidence_items.source_text: The initial ophthalmic examination demonstrated a best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 6/6 in the right eye and counting fingers (CF) at a distance of 0.5 feet in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was recorded at 12 mmHg in both eyes. Examination of the left eye revealed a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). The patient displayed full extraocular movements in both eyes. Anterior segment evaluation of the left eye was unremarkable.

However, dilated fundus examination revealed findings indicative of central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO), including optic disc edema, 360 degrees of preretinal hemorrhages, venous dilation and tortuosity, and cotton wool spots. Furthermore, a white ischemic area was observed nasally to the fovea, suggestive of a possible ciliary retinal artery occlusion (Fig. 1).
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed inner retinal hyperreflectivity (Fig. 2).

2Optical coherence tomography of the affected eye Furthermore, fluorescein fundus angiography (FFA) revealed delayed dye filling of the ciliary retinal artery, with a masking effect due to preretinal hemorrhages in the left eye.
On the basis of these findings, she was clinically diagnosed with central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) accompanied by ciliary retinal artery (CLRA) occlusion secondary to OCPs.

The patient was given acetazolamide, aspirin, ocular massage, and a combination of dorzolamide and timolol. She was monitored biweekly to assess visual acuity and intraocular pressure (IOP) for 12 weeks, followed by evaluations every 8 weeks for 6 months, then biannual check-ups for 2 years. At 6 weeks, after resolution of the preretinal hemorrhages, panretinal photocoagulation was performed to prevent neovascular glaucoma, which is associated with central retinal vein occlusion within 90 days. It was performed prophylactically as the patient resides in a remote area and was unwilling to adhere to a regular follow-up schedule. Intravitreal antivascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) was not used, as no macular edema was observed on OCT. By the 12th week, the patient’s vision was 6/36, with an IOP of 12 mmHg in the left eye.

Investigations for congenital and acquired thrombophilia, such as prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), international normalized ratio (INR), antiphospholipid antibodies, and factor V Leiden mutation yielded normal results. The patient also did not have other common risk factors such as diabetes, hyperlipidemia, or autoimmune conditions. Her autoimmune profile was normal. No plaque or thrombus was noted on carotid Doppler ultrasonography. Echocardiography was also unremarkable. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound reports were unremarkable. No sign of retinal vascular inflammation was noted on slit lamp biomicroscopy.
